name: Workflow
vision: Break complex work into subtasks, manage the dependencies between them, and assemble the results.
question: An agent workflow cut the first four design-thinking stages by 46% and did worse at reading users' emotions (Choi et al.). Which subtasks should stay with people?

name: Task assignment
vision: Match workers to tasks that fit their skills and interests, so requesters get speed and workers stay steadily employed.
question: 29% of tasks across the U.S. economy are already exposed to AI, a share growing 49% a year (Wright et al.). Who decides which tasks stay with people?

name: Hierarchy
vision: Crowd teams with managers and reviewers, so groups can take on large, complex work.
question: In Polymath Plus, an AI administers the discussion threads of human mathematicians (Michelucci et al.). When agents join a team, who manages whom?

name: Real-time response
vision: Crowds on call that respond within seconds for work that cannot wait.
question: AI support is immediate, and it lacks the lived experience that makes peer support meaningful (Goel et al.). When do we still need people on call?

name: Synchronous collaboration
vision: Strangers build rapport fast enough to work together on a task within an hour.
question: Entrepreneurs turned to peers to verify AI-written business plans they could not judge alone (Zhao et al.). What does working together add when everyone has AI?

name: Quality control
vision: Keep work quality high, including for open-ended and expert tasks where no gold standard exists.
question: Fluent AI explanations lead moderators to follow the AI even when it errs (Tuo et al.). Who catches AI failures, and how do teams calibrate trust?

name: Crowds guiding AIs
vision: People do the work AI systems cannot yet do. The paper warned that workers “may end up training machines to replace them.”
question: LLMs reach near-human accuracy on objective annotation and remain error-prone on subjective tasks (Xu et al.). Who holds the harness when AI fails, bug-bounty style?

name: AIs guiding crowds
vision: Software steers crowd work, catching errors before they spread through the crowd.
question: Annotation quality showed no clear difference between crowdworkers instructed by AI and by people (Libreros et al.). Where should people still steer?

name: Platforms
vision: New platforms that reshape the relationship between workers and requesters.
question: MTurk sunsets on September 30, 2026, the last day of this conference (After MTurk panel). What replaces it, and what do workers get?

name: Job design
vision: Work that builds skills and meaning, well beyond dull piecework dressed up as a game.
question: Some work is ‘non-delegable’: its value lies in human responsibility and presence (Gupta). What work beside AI would we be proud to see our children do?

name: Reputation and credentials
vision: Lasting, portable reputation, like references and work histories in traditional firms.
question: Once AI help was removed, people did worse than their AI-assisted results suggested (Wu et al.). How do you build a track record when AI did half the work?

name: Motivation and rewards
vision: Rewards matched to workers’ diverse motives and ambitions, beyond small payments per task.
question: On a 2026 bounty market, posted prices hide what workers must reveal to get paid (YeckehZaare). What should overseeing AI pay, and what if tokens stop being cheap?

name: Governance and the social contract
vision: Missing from the 2013 framework. Proposed at CrowdCamp 2026: a social contract between people, technology and the environment, with collective action as a counterweight to AI.
question: A workshop here asks that affected communities hold ‘meaningful authority over outcomes’ (Ku & Wu). Who writes the social contract? Can crowds organize the way unions once did?
